title: Eliminating an unknown by differences
transcript: When two totals share the same contribution, subtracting them removes that contribution. The difference isolates the part that changed. Put a label on each unknown before you use a symbol. As you work, keep the same label attached to the same quantity.

In AMC Upper Primary practice, look for bundles with matching parts or clues about what extra objects cost. A diagram or short equation can collect the clues in one place. In a Rossmoyne style puzzle, two or more conditions can constrain the same value. Substitute your result into the original conditions to prove it fits.
One bun and two drinks cost twenty-one dollars. Two buns and two drinks cost twenty-six dollars. Find the price of a bun. Compare what changed between the orders.
The two drinks occur in both orders, so their total price cancels. Only one additional bun remains. The price increase is five dollars. That is the cost of one bun.
Three pens and one marker cost twenty-three dollars. Four pens and two markers cost thirty-six dollars. Find each price. Create two orders with the same number of markers first.

Double the first bundle to make six pens and two markers costing forty-six. Subtract the second bundle. The difference is two pens costing ten. One pen costs five dollars. Substitute into the first order to get eight dollars for a marker.

A stall sells two kinds of pack, X and Y. An order of four X packs and two Y packs costs thirty-six dollars. An order of seven X packs and three Y packs costs fifty-nine dollars. Find each unit price.

The smaller number of Y packs in a common scaled order is six. Multiply the first entire equation by three and the second by two. Subtract the scaled first equation from the scaled second. That leaves two times X equal to ten. Dividing gives five dollars for X. Putting that into the first condition gives eight dollars for Y.

Rebuild both purchases. The first costs thirty-six and the second costs fifty-nine dollars. The difference equation had a nonzero coefficient for X. That forced its price before we substituted to find Y.

The other parts must match before they cancel. Scale an equation if the two numbers of matching objects differ. Multiplying an equation scales every coefficient and the total on the other side by the same factor.

Name the unknown quantity and write what each given relationship says about it. Label your equations with the units used in the story. Recheck the result by applying the original relationships, including each bound, whole-number rule or shared total.
